title: New Frontiers
bigQuestion: How should we decide which new medical powers to use, for whom, and with what care?

story.title: One Edit, One Life
story.kicker: In 2019 a woman from Mississippi became the first person in the United States treated for sickle cell disease with CRISPR-edited cells.
paragraphs: Victoria Gray grew up in Mississippi with sickle cell disease. Her body made red blood cells that could bend into stiff crescent shapes. Those cells got stuck in small blood vessels. When they did, she felt waves of pain so strong that she often ended up in the hospital. As a child she missed school, birthday parties and ordinary days with friends. She learned to plan her life around the next crisis.

In 2019, at a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee, she joined a clinical trial. Doctors collected her own blood-forming stem cells. In a laboratory, scientists used a tool called CRISPR to make one precise cut in the DNA of those cells. The cut switched back on a kind of hemoglobin that babies make before birth. This fetal hemoglobin does not sickle. Then the edited cells went back into her body.

The treatment was hard. Before the cells returned, she received strong chemotherapy to clear space in her bone marrow. She spent weeks in the hospital. Then, slowly, her blood changed. Her body began making healthy amounts of fetal hemoglobin. The pain crises that had shaped her whole life became rare. News reporters followed her story, and she spoke about being able to plan a future.

In December 2023 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved this kind of treatment for sickle cell disease. It was the first approved medicine in the country built on CRISPR. It is also very expensive and needs a major hospital stay. So Victoria Gray's story raises two questions at once. What can new medicine do? And who will be able to get it?
story.think: Victoria Gray's treatment worked for her, but it is costly and hard to go through. What should doctors, families and governments weigh before offering a new treatment like this to many people?

lessons.title: How mRNA Vaccines Work
lessons.mainIdea: An mRNA vaccine gives cells short-lived instructions to make one harmless piece of a germ, so the immune system learns to recognize it.
reading: In December 2020, nurses in the United States began giving the first COVID-19 vaccines. Two of the first vaccines used a new method called *mRNA*. The idea had taken researchers about thirty years to make work. The vaccines were built within days once the virus's genetic code was shared, and then they were tested in large trials with tens of thousands of volunteers.

Your cells use messenger RNA, or mRNA, as a working copy of a gene. The copy carries instructions to the cell's protein-making machinery. An mRNA vaccine delivers instructions for just one protein, the spike protein on the outside of the coronavirus. Cells make that protein for a short time. The mRNA breaks down within days, and it does not enter the cell's nucleus or change DNA.

The immune system sees the spike protein and treats it as foreign. It makes *antibodies*, proteins that stick to the spike, and it trains memory cells. If the real virus arrives later, the body is ready faster. Hungarian-born scientist Katalin Karikó and American scientist Drew Weissman found a way to change mRNA so it did not set off too much inflammation. They shared the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for that work.

words.d: messenger RNA; a short-lived working copy of a gene that tells a cell which protein to make
proteins made by the immune system that attach to a specific germ or germ part
the protein on the outside of the coronavirus that helps it enter cells
a careful study that tests a treatment in volunteers, often against a comparison group

look.title: A Recipe Card, Not a Cookbook
look.text: Picture a busy kitchen. The full cookbook stays locked in the office. A cook gets one recipe card, makes one dish, and throws the card away. The office cookbook never changes. In a cell, the DNA in the nucleus is the cookbook. An mRNA vaccine is one recipe card that gets used for a short time and then breaks down.
look.prompt: Use the kitchen picture to explain to a worried relative why an mRNA vaccine does not change a person's DNA.

check.q: What does an mRNA vaccine tell cells to make?
choices: One harmless protein from the germ, such as the spike protein
A complete, living copy of the virus
New DNA for the cell's nucleus
check.why: The reading says the vaccine carries instructions for just one protein, the spike, not a whole virus or new DNA.

check.q: What happens to the vaccine's mRNA after the cell uses it?
choices: It stays in the body for life
It moves into the nucleus and joins the DNA
check.why: The reading states that the mRNA breaks down within days and does not enter the nucleus.

check.q: Why did Karikó and Weissman win the 2023 Nobel Prize?
choices: They found a way to change mRNA so it caused less inflammation
check.why: The reading credits them with changing mRNA so it did not set off too much inflammation.

lessons.title: CRISPR: Editing a Gene
lessons.mainIdea: CRISPR lets scientists cut DNA at a chosen spot, which makes it possible to change a gene far more precisely than before.
reading: Bacteria have enemies too: viruses that attack them. Many bacteria keep small pieces of old virus DNA in their own DNA, like mug shots. If the same virus returns, the bacterium makes a guide that matches it and sends a cutting protein, such as Cas9, to cut the invader's DNA. Scientists named this system *CRISPR*, from the repeating pattern of DNA where the mug shots are stored.

In 2012, Jennifer Doudna of the University of California, Berkeley, and Emmanuelle Charpentier, a French microbiologist, showed that this system could be turned into a tool. Scientists can write a *guide RNA* that matches almost any stretch of DNA they choose. The guide leads Cas9 to that spot, and Cas9 cuts. The cell then repairs the cut, and researchers can use that repair to switch a gene off or change it. Doudna and Charpentier won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Victoria Gray's treatment shows how this works in medicine. Scientists did not fix the sickle cell gene itself. They cut a switch gene that normally turns off fetal hemoglobin after birth. With that switch cut, her blood cells made fetal hemoglobin again. This is called *somatic* editing: it changes cells in one patient's body, and those changes are not passed to children.

words.d: a gene-editing system, first found in bacteria, that cuts DNA at a spot chosen by a guide
a short piece of RNA that leads the cutting protein to the matching stretch of DNA
the protein in the most common CRISPR system that cuts DNA
having to do with body cells that are not passed on to children

look.title: Find and Replace
look.text: A student types a 300-page report and misspells one name everywhere. She uses Find to jump straight to the word, then fixes it. Older gene methods were more like dropping new pages into the report at random places. CRISPR works more like Find: the guide RNA searches for one exact phrase in billions of letters of DNA, and Cas9 cuts right there.
look.prompt: The Find tool sometimes stops at a word that only looks like the one you want. What might a similar mistake mean for a gene edit, and why would researchers test for it?

check.q: Where did the CRISPR system first come from?
check.why: The reading explains that bacteria use CRISPR to recognize and cut the DNA of viruses that attacked them before.

check.q: What is the job of the guide RNA?
choices: To lead Cas9 to the matching spot in the DNA
To carry oxygen in the blood
check.why: The guide RNA matches a chosen stretch of DNA and leads Cas9 there to cut.

check.q: In Victoria Gray's treatment, what did the edit do?
choices: It removed her red blood cells
It turned fetal hemoglobin back on by cutting a switch gene
It changed the DNA of her future children
It gave her an mRNA vaccine
check.why: Scientists cut a switch gene so her cells made fetal hemoglobin again; the edit was somatic, not passed to children.

lessons.title: The Ethics of Editing
lessons.mainIdea: Editing body cells to treat one patient is widely accepted with care, while editing embryos that pass changes to future generations remains strongly contested.
reading: In November 2018, a Chinese scientist named He Jiankui announced that twin girls had been born from embryos he had edited with CRISPR. He said he wanted to protect them from HIV. Scientists around the world objected. The work had not been openly reviewed, the risks were unknown, and the edits could pass to the girls' own children. A Chinese court later sentenced him to prison for illegal medical practice.

The key difference is between somatic editing and *germline* editing. Germline editing changes eggs, sperm or embryos, so every cell of the future person carries the change, and so can that person's children. Many scientists and ethicists say germline editing should not be used to start pregnancies now. They point to unknown safety risks and to the fact that future people cannot give *consent*, which means agreeing after understanding the risks.

Others argue that one day germline editing might prevent serious inherited diseases for a whole family line. There are also worries about fairness: if editing becomes a costly option for the wealthy, it could widen gaps in health. These are real, open debates. Most countries restrict germline editing, and international scientific meetings have called for strict limits and broad public discussion before any use.

words.d: eggs, sperm and early embryos; changes to them can be passed to future generations
agreement given freely by a person who understands the risks and benefits
the study of what is right and fair, and how people should act

look.title: Scientists Draw a Line
look.text: The organizers of the first international summit on human gene editing said that basic research and somatic uses should go forward under rules. They said it would be irresponsible to use germline editing in pregnancies until safety questions were answered and society broadly agreed that it was appropriate.
look.cite: Organizing Committee, International Summit on Human Gene Editing, statement, Washington, D.C., December 2015 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: The summit set two conditions. Name them, and explain why He Jiankui's 2018 work did not meet either one.

check.q: Why did He Jiankui's 2018 experiment alarm scientists?
choices: He used mRNA instead of CRISPR
He edited embryos whose changes could pass to future children, without open review
He treated adults with sickle cell disease
He refused to publish any results at all about anyone
check.why: He edited embryos (germline) in secret, with unknown risks and changes that could be inherited.

check.q: Which describes germline editing?
choices: Changing cells in one patient's blood only
Changing eggs, sperm or embryos so changes can be inherited
check.why: Germline editing affects eggs, sperm or embryos, so the change can pass to later generations.

check.q: What fairness concern does the lesson raise about gene editing?
choices: It could widen health gaps if only wealthy people can pay for it
It is illegal in every country for all uses
check.why: The reading notes that costly editing could widen gaps in health between rich and poor.

lessons.title: Personalized Medicine
lessons.mainIdea: Personalized medicine uses a person's genes and the features of their illness to choose the treatment most likely to help them.
reading: Two women have breast cancer. Under the microscope their tumors look alike. But a lab test shows that one tumor has large amounts of a protein called HER2 on its cells. For her, doctors can add a drug called trastuzumab, which targets HER2. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved it in 1998. For the other woman, whose tumor lacks extra HER2, that drug would not help.

This is *personalized medicine*, sometimes called precision medicine. Instead of one treatment for everyone with the same disease name, doctors use tests to find which group a patient belongs to. It became much more practical after the Human Genome Project finished reading nearly all of human DNA in 2003. Since then, reading a person's genes has become far faster and cheaper.

One branch is *pharmacogenomics*, the study of how genes affect a person's response to medicines. Some people's livers break down certain drugs quickly, and others slowly. A gene test can help a doctor choose a medicine or a safer starting amount. Personalized medicine is growing, but many tests are costly, and most studies so far have included mostly people of European ancestry, so results may not fit everyone equally well.

words.d: choosing care based on a person's genes, test results and illness features; also called precision medicine
the study of how a person's genes affect how they respond to medicines
all of the DNA in an organism
something that can be measured, like a protein, that shows a feature of a disease

look.title: One Size, Many Bodies
look.text: A shoe store sells only one size, size 9. It fits many customers well. For others it pinches or slips. Now the store measures each foot first and offers several sizes. For decades, many medicines were tested and dosed as if most patients wore size 9. Personalized medicine tries to measure first.
look.prompt: The lesson says most genetic studies have included mostly people of European ancestry. Using the shoe store picture, explain why that is a problem and what could fix it.

check.q: Why can trastuzumab help one breast cancer patient but not another?
choices: It only works on tumors with large amounts of the HER2 protein
check.why: The reading says trastuzumab targets HER2, so it helps tumors with extra HER2 and not others.

check.q: What does pharmacogenomics study?
choices: How a person's genes affect their response to medicines
check.why: Pharmacogenomics studies how genes shape the way a person responds to drugs.

check.q: What limit of personalized medicine does the lesson name?
choices: It has never helped any patient
It is only used in traditional medicine
Many studies have mostly included people of European ancestry
check.why: The reading warns that mostly European-ancestry study groups mean results may not fit everyone equally.

lessons.title: AI in Diagnosis
lessons.mainIdea: Artificial intelligence can find patterns in medical images and records, but it needs testing, fair data and human oversight.
reading: People with diabetes can slowly lose vision from damage to the blood vessels in the retina, the back of the eye. Catching it early helps. In 2018 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration authorized a system called IDx-DR. A trained staff member photographs the retina in a regular clinic. Software then decides whether the patient should see an eye specialist, without a specialist first reading the picture.

This software is a kind of *artificial intelligence*, or AI. It was built through *machine learning*: a computer program studied a very large number of labeled eye photographs until it could sort new ones. Similar tools now help flag possible problems on X-rays, skin photos and heart tracings. Many work best as a second pair of eyes that points a doctor toward something to check.

AI has real limits. A program learns only from the data it is given. If most training images came from one group of people, it may make more mistakes with others; this is called *algorithmic bias*. A program can also be confidently wrong. For these reasons, health bodies stress testing tools in real clinics, protecting patient privacy, and keeping trained people responsible for decisions.

words.d: computer systems that do tasks that usually need human judgment, such as sorting images
a way of building AI in which a program learns patterns from many examples
unfair errors in a computer program, often caused by training data that leaves some groups out
the light-sensing layer at the back of the eye

look.title: Rules for Health AI
look.text: The World Health Organization set out principles for AI in health. People should stay in control of health decisions. Tools should be safe and well tested. How they work should be explained clearly. Someone should be accountable. They should be fair to all groups, and they should be responsive and sustainable over time.
look.cite: World Health Organization, Ethics and Governance of Artificial Intelligence for Health, 2021 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Pick one principle from the WHO list. Explain how it would apply to the eye-screening software in the lesson.

check.q: What did the IDx-DR system authorized in 2018 do?
choices: Read retina photos to find diabetic eye disease that needs a specialist
Replace all eye doctors in the United States
check.why: The reading says the software reads retina photos and decides whether a patient should see an eye specialist.

check.q: How is a machine-learning program built?
choices: It is written by hand one rule at a time
It learns patterns from a very large number of labeled examples
check.why: Machine learning means the program studies many labeled examples and learns to sort new ones.

check.q: What can cause algorithmic bias?
choices: Training data that leaves some groups of people out
check.why: If the training data mostly comes from one group, the program can make more mistakes with others.

lessons.title: Care Across Distance
lessons.mainIdea: Telehealth brings some care to patients by video, phone and messages, which helps many people but does not replace every in-person visit.
reading: In spring 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic closed many clinic waiting rooms. Almost overnight, a large share of doctor visits in the United States moved to video and phone calls. A teenager could talk with a counselor from her bedroom. An older farmer could review blood-pressure readings with a nurse without driving two hours to town.

This is *telehealth*: health care delivered at a distance using technology. It includes video visits, phone calls, secure messages and *remote monitoring*, in which a device at home, such as a blood-pressure cuff or glucose meter, sends readings to a care team. Telehealth can save travel time, reach rural areas with few specialists, and make follow-up visits easier to keep.

Telehealth also has limits. A doctor cannot listen to lungs or press on a sore belly through a screen, so some problems still need an in-person exam. Not every home has fast internet, a private room or a device, a gap often called the *digital divide*. Many clinics now mix the two: video for check-ins and talk therapy, and in-person visits for exams, tests and emergencies.

words.d: health care and health information delivered at a distance using video, phone or messages
using a device at home to send health readings to a care team
the gap between people who have good internet and devices and people who do not

look.title: Screen or Room?
look.text: Three patients call a clinic on the same morning. Jordan, 16, wants to check in with his counselor about stress at school. Mrs. Lopez, 72, has a new, sharp pain in her lower right belly. Mr. Tan, 55, needs to go over a week of home blood-pressure readings with his nurse.
look.prompt: For each patient, would you suggest telehealth or an in-person visit? Give one reason from the lesson for each choice.

check.q: Which is an example of remote monitoring?
choices: A surgeon operating in a hospital
A home glucose meter that sends readings to a care team
A student reading a health textbook
check.why: Remote monitoring means a device at home sends health readings to the care team.

check.q: What event caused a sudden rise in telehealth in the United States?
check.why: The reading says many visits moved to video and phone in spring 2020 during COVID-19.

check.q: What does the digital divide mean?
choices: The split between doctors and nurses
A line between two hospital buildings
The gap between people with good internet and devices and people without
check.why: The digital divide is the gap in access to internet, devices and private space for video care.

lessons.title: When Antibiotics Stop Working
lessons.mainIdea: Bacteria can evolve resistance to antibiotics, so using antibiotics only when needed helps keep them working.
reading: When Alexander Fleming accepted the Nobel Prize in 1945 for discovering penicillin, he gave a warning. If people took too little penicillin, or took it when it was not needed, surviving bacteria could become resistant. He had already seen this happen in his laboratory. Within a few years, doctors began finding resistant bacteria in hospitals.

*Antibiotic resistance* happens through natural selection. In a large group of bacteria, a few may carry a gene change that helps them survive a drug. The antibiotic kills the others, and the survivors multiply. Bacteria can even pass resistance genes to one another. Antibiotics work against bacteria only; they do nothing against viruses, such as those that cause colds and flu.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported in 2019 that more than 2.8 million antibiotic-resistant infections happen in the United States each year, and more than 35,000 people die from them. Helpful steps are known. Take antibiotics only when a clinician prescribes them. Take them exactly as directed. Wash hands and keep vaccines up to date. This practice of careful use is called *antibiotic stewardship*.

words.d: the ability of bacteria to survive drugs that used to kill them
the process in which living things with helpful traits survive and reproduce more
careful use of antibiotics only when needed and exactly as directed, to keep them working

look.title: Fleming's Warning
look.text: Fleming said a time might come when anyone could buy penicillin in a shop. He worried that a person might take too small an amount, so that the germs were not killed but taught to resist it. Then that person could pass a resistant germ to someone else.
look.prompt: Fleming spoke in 1945. Which part of his warning matches what the CDC reported in 2019?

check.q: According to the lesson, how does resistance spread in a group of bacteria?
choices: The antibiotic teaches every bacterium to resist
Viruses give bacteria resistance on purpose
A few bacteria with helpful gene changes survive the drug and multiply
Resistance only appears in people who never take antibiotics
check.why: This is natural selection: survivors with a helpful gene change multiply after the drug kills the rest.

check.q: Why do antibiotics not help with a common cold?
choices: Colds are caused by viruses, and antibiotics work only on bacteria
Colds are too mild for medicine
Colds are caused by resistant bacteria
check.why: The reading states that antibiotics work only against bacteria and do nothing against viruses.

check.q: Which is an example of antibiotic stewardship?
choices: Saving leftover antibiotics for next time
Sharing antibiotics with a sick friend
Asking for antibiotics for every cough
Taking antibiotics only when prescribed and exactly as directed
check.why: Stewardship means careful use: only when a clinician prescribes it, and exactly as directed.

lessons.title: A World Growing Older
lessons.mainIdea: People are living longer, so health systems are planning for more older adults, many of whom live with long-term conditions.
reading: In Japan, one of the countries with the longest life expectancy, it is common to meet healthy people in their eighties still gardening and walking to the market. Around the world, the same shift is under way. Better sanitation, vaccines, safer childbirth and treatment for heart disease mean more people reach old age than ever before.

The World Health Organization estimates that about 1 billion people were aged 60 or older in 2020. It projects about 1.4 billion by 2030 and about 2.1 billion by 2050. This is called *population aging*. Older adults are more likely to live with *chronic conditions*, illnesses that last a long time, such as arthritis, heart disease, diabetes or dementia. Many have more than one.

Aging well is not only about treating disease. The WHO speaks of *healthy aging*: helping people keep doing what they value. Regular movement, social contact, good hearing and vision care, and fall prevention all help. Health systems will need more geriatric specialists, nurses, home-care workers and family caregivers, and communities will need safe sidewalks, transit and places to gather.

words.d: a rise in the share of older people in a population
an illness or health problem that lasts a long time, often for life
the WHO's idea of helping older people keep the abilities to do what they value
the average number of years people born in a place and time are expected to live

look.title: People Aged 60 and Older, Worldwide
look.cite: World Health Organization, Ageing and Health fact sheet, 2022
look.prompt: About how many more people aged 60 or older does the WHO expect in 2050 than in 2020? Name one job or service that will be needed more.

check.q: About how many people worldwide does the WHO expect to be 60 or older in 2050?
check.why: The WHO projection in the lesson is about 2.1 billion people aged 60 or older by 2050.

check.q: What is a chronic condition?
choices: An illness that lasts a long time, such as arthritis or diabetes
An injury that heals in a day
check.why: Chronic conditions are long-lasting illnesses like arthritis, heart disease or diabetes.

check.q: Which step supports healthy aging, according to the lesson?
check.why: The lesson lists regular movement, social contact, hearing and vision care and fall prevention.

lessons.title: Caring at the Bedside
lessons.mainIdea: Nurses, doctors, pharmacists, therapists and EMTs each do different work and need different training and a state license.
reading: Follow one patient, a man who falls from a ladder. Emergency medical technicians, or *EMTs*, reach him first. They check his breathing, protect his neck and drive him to the hospital. EMT training is a course of a few months, followed by a certification exam. Paramedics train longer and can give more medicines.

At the hospital, a registered nurse watches him hour by hour, gives medicines and explains what is happening. Registered nurses earn a two-year associate degree or a four-year bachelor's degree and then pass a national licensing exam, the NCLEX-RN. A physician diagnoses his broken hip. Physicians finish four years of college, four years of medical school, and then *residency*, supervised hospital training that lasts about three to seven years.

Before he goes home, a pharmacist checks that his new medicines are safe together. Pharmacists earn a Doctor of Pharmacy degree and pass licensing exams. A physical therapist helps him walk again; physical therapists earn a doctoral degree, usually three years after college. Each of these jobs requires a *license*, official permission from a state to practice.

words.d: emergency medical technician; a trained worker who gives urgent care before and on the way to a hospital
a licensed nurse who cares for patients, gives medicines and teaches patients and families
supervised hospital training for new doctors after medical school
official permission from a state to work in a health profession

look.title: Typical Minimum Years of Study After High School
look.cite: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Outlook Handbook, 2024
look.prompt: Which two paths differ most in training time? Name one reason a student might pick either one.

check.q: Which worker usually reaches an injured person first and gives care on the way to the hospital?
check.why: The lesson says EMTs reach the patient first and care for him on the way to the hospital.

check.q: What is residency?
choices: Supervised hospital training for new doctors after medical school
check.why: Residency is supervised hospital training that follows medical school, lasting about three to seven years.

check.q: What does a pharmacist do for the patient in the lesson?
choices: Checks that his new medicines are safe together
check.why: The pharmacist checks that the new medicines are safe to take together.

lessons.title: Research, Public Health and More
lessons.mainIdea: Many health careers work behind the scenes or in communities, and some traditional practices, like acupuncture, are licensed by most states.
reading: Not every health worker sees patients one at a time. Some are *researchers*. Katalin Karikó spent decades in laboratories studying mRNA before it became a vaccine. Research careers usually need a doctoral degree, such as a PhD or MD, and years of work in a lab or clinic. Research assistants and lab technicians help run studies with less schooling.

*Public health* workers protect the health of whole communities. They track outbreaks, inspect restaurants, test water and run vaccination drives. When a city health department traces the spread of measles, public-health workers are doing the detective work. Many hold a Master of Public Health degree, and community health workers often begin with shorter training and deep ties to the neighborhoods they serve.

Health care also includes other licensed paths. An *acupuncturist* practices a therapy from Traditional Chinese Medicine. Most U.S. states license acupuncturists; they usually complete a master's-level program and a national certification exam. Other careers include dietitians, respiratory therapists, occupational therapists, medical interpreters and dental hygienists. Rules differ from state to state, so a smart first step is to check your own state's licensing board.

words.d: a scientist who designs and runs studies to find new knowledge
the work of protecting and improving the health of whole communities
a practitioner who places thin needles in the skin, a therapy from Traditional Chinese Medicine
the state office that sets the rules and tests for a health profession

look.title: Three Students, Three Paths
look.text: Amara loves chemistry and does not mind long projects. Luis likes being out in his neighborhood and speaks English and Spanish. Keisha wants to help people right away after high school and stays calm in emergencies.
look.prompt: Suggest one health career for each student using the lessons, and name one thing each path needs, such as a degree, exam or license.

check.q: Which task is typical public-health work?
choices: Tracing how measles is spreading in a city
check.why: Public-health workers protect whole communities, including tracking outbreaks like measles.

check.q: How are acupuncturists regulated in the United States?
choices: They are not allowed to practice anywhere
Most states license them after a master's-level program and a national exam
Only the federal government licenses them
check.why: The lesson says most states license acupuncturists, who usually complete a master's-level program and a certification exam.

check.q: What does the lesson suggest as a smart first step for someone choosing a health career?
choices: Check your own state's licensing board
Pick the job with the shortest training
Wait until after college to learn about it
check.why: Rules differ by state, so the lesson suggests checking your state's licensing board.

review.q: What made Victoria Gray's treatment for sickle cell disease possible?
choices: CRISPR editing of her own blood-forming stem cells
review.why: Scientists used CRISPR to edit her stem cells so they made fetal hemoglobin again.

review.q: How are mRNA vaccines and CRISPR treatments different?
choices: mRNA vaccines briefly instruct cells to make a protein; CRISPR changes DNA
mRNA vaccines cut DNA; CRISPR trains antibodies
Neither has been tested in people
review.why: mRNA is a short-lived instruction that does not touch DNA, while CRISPR cuts and changes DNA.

review.q: Why is germline editing more contested than somatic editing?
choices: It has already been approved everywhere
Its changes can pass to future generations who cannot consent
review.why: Germline changes can be inherited, and future people cannot give consent to the risks.

review.q: A doctor orders a gene test to choose a safer starting medicine for a patient. What is this an example of?
review.why: Pharmacogenomics uses genes to predict how a person will respond to a medicine.

review.q: Why do health bodies insist that people stay responsible for decisions made with AI tools?
choices: AI can be confidently wrong and can carry bias from its training data
review.why: The AI lesson says programs can be confidently wrong and biased, so human oversight is needed.

review.q: Which situation still needs an in-person visit rather than telehealth?
choices: A new sharp belly pain that needs an exam
review.why: A doctor cannot press on a sore belly through a screen, so new belly pain needs an in-person exam.

review.q: What did Alexander Fleming warn about in 1945?
choices: That vaccines would replace all antibiotics
That misusing penicillin could breed resistant bacteria
review.why: In his Nobel lecture Fleming warned that too little or needless penicillin could make bacteria resistant.

review.q: Which health career usually needs the longest training after high school?
choices: Registered nurse with an associate degree
review.why: Physicians complete college, medical school and three to seven years of residency, about 11 or more years.
